answer.rationale:
The tempting move is the one memory_c2 endorses: switch primary supply to the low-cost vendor, whose quote alone satisfies the 18% mandate. That is exactly why memory_c2 is worth pulling. It is the load-bearing record for the highest-consequence option, it is dated ('last year'), and its supporting detail is thin on the dimension that matters now: it praises fast onboarding and accurate invoicing, not sustained on-time delivery at volume. A switch executed with 14 days of runway, the line at 94% of committed volume, and no buffer means any onboarding slip converts directly into missed commitments. Cost mandate met, delivery risk raised — which violates the stated objective. Second pull is memory_c4, because renegotiation is the option that could hit the cost target without touching the physical supply path, and I want to know what actually moved the incumbent (benchmark data, volume leverage, timing) so I can reproduce the mechanism rather than the outcome.

Intended action: negotiate terms with the incumbent, benchmarked against the low-cost quote, on a short commitment. This uses the low-cost quote as leverage rather than as a migration. memory_c1 says the incumbent relationship held integration stable across two cycles, so the no-migration path protects the 94% line. memory_c6 shows multi-year commitments unlock volume pricing, but I am deliberately not taking that route this cycle — locking multi-year while the low-cost vendor's real delivery reliability is unverified would trade away the option to switch later once I have capacity to qualify them properly. Hence small and guarded: short term, cost relief now, switch option preserved.

Uncertainty I am not resolving: whether the low-cost vendor can hold allocation at committed volume, and whether renegotiation can close the full 18% or only part of it. If the archive shows memory_c4's savings came from a mechanism unavailable here, or that the incumbent's recovered margin was small, the fallback is add_second_source at low volume to qualify the low-cost vendor without betting the line — consistent with memory_c3, where dual sourcing held allocation through a shortage. memory_c5 (defer) is not viable: this contract does not auto-renew, so deferring means lapsing supply, not extending it month-to-month.
